opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Picasso came from a pretty simple observation. By around 2022, it was clear that visual generative AI, meaning image, video, and eventually 3D generation, was going to become a very important technology. But for most companies, especially those in the creative industry, building these models from scratch was extremely hard. You need a lot of compute, a lot of expertise in model design and training, and you need data that you actually have the rights to use.

So with Picasso, we wanted to create a foundry. Just like a semiconductor foundry helps customers manufacture chips they design, we wanted to help enterprises build their own custom visual generative models. NVIDIA would provide the model architectures, which we called Edify, the training recipes, the infrastructure, and the optimized inference. The partners would bring their own data and their own domain knowledge.

A big part of it was about doing generative AI responsibly. We worked with partners like Getty Images and Shutterstock, who have large libraries of licensed content, so the models could be trained on data where the contributors are compensated and the outputs are commercially safe for their customers. In the creative world that matters a lot. If you're a brand or an agency, you need to know you can actually use what you generate.

From the research side, it was also a chance to push the technology forward: better image quality, higher resolution, better text-to-image alignment, and then moving into video and 3D assets. For me personally, it connected back to earlier work like GauGAN, where the dream was always to give people a tool that turns imagination into visual content very quickly. Picasso was a way to take that research dream and make it something industry could really build products on.

r001.rationale: The response says Picasso would help enterprises build custom visual generative models using their own data and expertise, addressing the compute and model-building expertise that made building from scratch difficult.

r002.rationale: It describes NVIDIA providing architectures, training, infrastructure, and inference, and says partners bring data. It does not clearly state that partners would use NVIDIA-built models to serve their own customers.

r003.rationale: The response connects earlier research to products industry could build, but does not clearly state that developing those products helped customers succeed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. With Picasso, the core idea was pretty simple: we didn't think the right model for generative AI in the enterprise was one company training one giant model and everyone else just calling an API. We thought of it more like a foundry.

In the semiconductor world, a foundry doesn't design your chip for you. You bring your design, and the foundry provides the manufacturing capability you could never build yourself. We wanted to do the same thing for visual generative models. Companies like Getty Images, Shutterstock, Adobe have enormous libraries of images, video, 3D assets, and they have real questions about rights and licensing. They don't want to send that data somewhere and lose control, and they don't want a model trained on scraped data that might create legal exposure for their customers. So the goal was to give them pretrained foundation models, the training recipes, the optimized inference stack on top of DGX Cloud, and let them build their own models on their own licensed data.

For me personally, it also came out of the research. My group had spent years on GauGAN, on image-to-image translation, on neural rendering. We kept seeing that the research results were great, but the gap between a paper and something a company can actually deploy at scale was huge. Picasso was an attempt to close that gap, to turn the research into infrastructure.

And honestly, it was also about learning. By working with these partners we learned what enterprises actually need: controllability, consistency, provenance, the ability to fine-tune on a specific style. That shaped a lot of the thinking that later went into our world foundation model work. The ambition was never just text-to-image. It was to make generative AI a manufacturing capability that others could build on.

r001.rationale: The response says Picasso provided pretrained models, training recipes, and inference infrastructure so companies could build models on their own licensed data, using capabilities they could not build themselves.

r002.rationale: It describes partners building their own models, but does not say they would use NVIDIA-built models to serve their customers.

r003.rationale: It describes Picasso as turning Liu’s research into infrastructure that companies could deploy and build on, connecting research to practical enterprise use.

astra-6.text: The goal was to help companies build generative AI models tailored to their own needs. Rather than have every company build everything from scratch, we wanted to provide a foundation—the models, infrastructure, and expertise—that they could customize with their own data. For creative work, that meant giving artists and designers tools to explore ideas and create content more efficiently, while keeping them in control of the result.

r001.rationale: It says companies could customize generative AI models with their own data, but does not say this enabled companies without in-house AI capabilities to build them.

r002.rationale: It does not state that partner companies would use NVIDIA-built models to serve their own customers.

r003.rationale: It mentions creative tools, but does not describe Picasso as extending Liu’s research into products intended to help customers succeed.

sol-6.1.text: With Picasso, we wanted to help companies build generative AI models tailored to their own needs and data. Instead of every company having to develop everything from scratch, we would provide the foundation models, training infrastructure, and expertise so they could create and deploy their own tools for generating visual content. The idea was to give creators more control and make these capabilities useful in their existing workflows.

r001.rationale: The response says companies could tailor models to their data and receive infrastructure and expertise, but it does not clearly state that this enabled companies without in-house AI capabilities to do so.

r002.rationale: It says companies could create and deploy their own content-generation tools, but does not state that they would use models NVIDIA built for them to serve their own customers.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe Picasso as extending Ming-Yu Liu’s research into products designed to help customers succeed.
